terms: Design brief
Initial statement of the problem and requirements set by a client or identified through research, initiating the design process.
Evaluation
Critical review of a prototype against the specification, identifying improvements for the next iteration.
Iteration
Repeated cycle of designing, prototyping and testing that progressively refines a product based on feedback.
Prototype
Working or appearance model of a design used to test ideas, gather user feedback and refine specifications.
Specification
Set of measurable criteria a product must meet, covering function, materials, dimensions, cost and user needs.
User feedback
Information gathered from intended users through interviews, observation or testing, feeding decisions for iteration.
Critical path analysis
A project-planning technique identifying the longest chain of dependent tasks, which determines the minimum time the whole project can take.
Design for assembly
Designing parts that locate themselves, fit only the correct way and need few fasteners, reducing assembly time, errors and labour cost.
Design for manufacture (DFM)
Designing products so they are simpler and cheaper to make, by minimising part counts, using standard components and realistic tolerances.
Gantt chart
A bar chart plotting project tasks against time, showing durations, deadlines and which activities can run in parallel.
Quality control
Inspecting and testing products during manufacture against specified tolerances, for example using go/no-go gauges, to catch defects early.
Scales of production
One-off, batch, mass and continuous production; the chosen scale determines tooling investment, unit cost and suitable manufacturing processes.
As little design as possible
Rams's tenth principle advocating reduction to the essential, profoundly influencing Jonathan Ive's work at Apple.
Dieter Rams
German industrial designer chief of design at Braun from 1961 to 1995, whose products shaped consumer electronics aesthetics.
Honest design
Rams's principle that good design does not promise more than it can deliver, avoiding deceptive styling.
Innovative design
First of Rams's principles stating that good design uses new technological possibilities to develop genuinely original solutions.
Ten principles
Rams's list of qualities of good design, articulated in the 1970s and 1980s, including innovative, useful and aesthetic.
Useful design
Rams's principle that good design serves the user's needs, satisfying functional, psychological and aesthetic criteria.
Additive manufacturing
Building parts layer by layer from digital models, as in 3D printing, enabling complex geometries and rapid prototyping with little material waste.
CAD
Computer-aided design: producing 2D drawings and 3D models on screen, allowing rapid editing, accurate dimensioning and virtual testing before manufacture.
CAM
Computer-aided manufacture: using CAD data to drive machines such as routers, laser cutters and milling machines for accurate, repeatable production.
CNC
Computer numerical control: machine tools follow programmed coordinate instructions, often G-code, to cut identical parts with high precision.
Laser cutting
A subtractive CAM process using a focused laser beam to cut or engrave sheet materials quickly and with very high accuracy.
Virtual modelling and simulation
Testing a digital prototype on screen, for example simulating stresses or assembly, reducing the cost and number of physical prototypes.
Branding
The identity of a product or company — name, logo, values and reputation — built to create recognition, trust and customer loyalty.
Crowdfunding
Raising finance for a new product from many small contributors through online platforms, often pre-selling the product before manufacture.
Enterprise
Identifying a commercial opportunity and taking the financial risk of developing a new product or business to exploit it.
Market pull
Product development driven by consumer demand: designers respond to what the market asks for, such as healthier foods or smaller devices.
Market research
Gathering data about consumers through surveys, interviews and focus groups to identify needs, gaps in the market and likely demand.
Technology push
Product development driven by new technology or materials, where innovation creates products consumers did not know they wanted.
Hardwood
Timber from broadleaved deciduous trees such as oak and beech, generally denser and slower-growing than softwoods.
MDF
Medium-density fibreboard made from compressed wood fibres and resin, valued for smooth surfaces and ease of machining.
Manufactured board
Engineered timber product such as MDF, plywood or chipboard, providing dimensional stability and large sheet sizes.
Plywood
Manufactured board of thin veneers glued with grain at right angles, giving strength in both directions.
Seasoning
Controlled drying of timber to reduce moisture content, minimising warping and improving workability.
Softwood
Timber from coniferous trees such as pine and spruce, faster-growing and widely used for construction and furniture frames.
British Standard governing technical product documentation, defining how engineering drawings should be prepared.
British Standards Institution
UK national standards body founded in 1901 that publishes the BS series of standards.
CE marking
European conformity mark showing a product meets relevant EU health, safety and environmental requirements.
ISO standard
Standard published by the International Organization for Standardization, enabling consistency across global markets.
Kitemark
BSI certification mark indicating a product has been independently tested to meet a relevant British Standard.
UKCA marking
UK Conformity Assessed marking introduced in 2021 for goods placed on the Great Britain market after Brexit.

Die casting
Forcing molten metal, often zinc or aluminium alloy, into a reusable steel die to produce accurate, complex parts at volume.
Extrusion
Forcing heated material through a shaped die to create continuous lengths of constant cross-section, such as pipes, channels and rails.
Injection moulding
Melting thermoplastic granules and forcing them into a steel mould; very high tooling cost but extremely low unit cost at high volume.
Milling and turning
Machining processes: milling uses a rotating cutter on a fixed or moving workpiece, while turning rotates the workpiece against a tool on a lathe.
Sand casting
Pouring molten metal into an expendable sand mould; suited to one-off and small-batch parts such as machine bases.
Vacuum forming
Heating a thermoplastic sheet until soft, then drawing it over a mould with a vacuum; widely used for packaging and trays.
As little design as possible
Rams's tenth principle advocating reduction to the essential, profoundly influencing Jonathan Ive's work at Apple.
Dieter Rams
German industrial designer chief of design at Braun from 1961 to 1995, whose products shaped consumer electronics aesthetics.
Honest design
Rams's principle that good design does not promise more than it can deliver, avoiding deceptive styling.
Innovative design
First of Rams's principles stating that good design uses new technological possibilities to develop genuinely original solutions.
Ten principles
Rams's list of qualities of good design, articulated in the 1970s and 1980s, including innovative, useful and aesthetic.
Useful design
Rams's principle that good design serves the user's needs, satisfying functional, psychological and aesthetic criteria.
British Standards Institution (BSI)
The UK national standards body; its Kitemark shows a product has been independently tested against the relevant British Standard.
CE and UKCA marking
Conformity marks declaring a product meets essential safety requirements for sale in the European Union (CE) or Great Britain (UKCA).
Consumer Rights Act 2015
UK law requiring goods to be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described, giving buyers rights to repair, replacement or refund.
Patent
Legal protection for how an invention works, lasting up to 20 years in the UK, granted in exchange for publishing the invention's details.
Registered design
Protection for the visual appearance of a product — its shape, configuration and decoration — preventing competitors copying its look.
Trademark and copyright
A trademark protects brand identifiers such as names and logos; copyright automatically protects original creative works including drawings and text.
Design for disassembly
Design approach allowing products to be taken apart easily at end of life so components can be reused or recycled.
End-of-life planning
Consideration during design of how a product will be disposed of, reused or recycled, central to circular economy thinking.
Material separation
Practice of using compatible or easily separable materials in adjacent components, simplifying recycling streams.
Mechanical fasteners
Reversible fixings such as screws and clips, preferred over adhesives in design for disassembly to allow non-destructive separation.
Modular design
Structuring a product as exchangeable modules so failed parts can be replaced rather than the whole product discarded.
WEEE Directive
EU Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive (2003) requiring producers to fund collection and recycling of electronics.
Disruptive innovation
Clayton Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma 1997; low-end disruption (steel mini-mills) and new-market disruption (PCs).
Hype Cycle
Jackie Fenn Gartner 1995; technology trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, plateau of productivity.
Kondratiev waves
Nikolai Kondratiev 1925 long economic cycles of 45-60 years driven by major innovations: steam, rail, electricity, automobile, IT.
Moore's Law
Gordon Moore Electronics Magazine 1965; transistor count doubles every two years; held roughly true for five decades.
S-curve adoption
Everett Rogers's Diffusion of Innovations 1962; innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards form bell distribution.
TRL scale
NASA 1974 Technology Readiness Level 1-9; from basic principles to flight proven; adopted by US DOD 1999 and EU H2020 2014.
Aesthetic analysis
Examination of how visual qualities such as form, colour and texture contribute to a product's appeal and identity.
Cost analysis
Breakdown of materials, manufacture and overheads contributing to retail price, identifying where margins arise.
Disassembly
Taking a product apart to examine its components, materials and construction, revealing design and manufacturing decisions.
Function analysis
Identification of a product's primary and secondary functions, separating essential from desirable features.
Materials analysis
Identification of materials used in a product and evaluation of why each was selected for its role.
Reverse engineering
Detailed analysis of an existing product to understand its design and reproduce or improve it.
Batch production
Manufacture of a limited quantity of identical products before retooling for the next batch, balancing flexibility and efficiency.
Cell production
Manufacturing organisation grouping equipment into cells where teams complete identifiable units, improving flexibility and morale.
Continuous production
Manufacturing running 24/7 to produce uninterrupted output, used in industries such as glass, chemicals and electricity generation.
Just-in-time
Production system minimising stock by delivering components as needed, developed by Toyota in the 1970s.
Mass production
Continuous large-scale manufacture of standardised products, pioneered for cars by Henry Ford's Model T line in 1913.
One-off production
Manufacture of a single unique product, used for bespoke commissions; labour-intensive but flexible.
Appearance prototype
Cosmetic prototype representing the look of a final product without necessarily being functional.
Block model
Solid foam or timber model representing the overall mass and ergonomics of a product, often used in product design studios.
Card model
Quick prototype made from card and adhesive, exploring overall form and scale early in the design process.
Iterative prototyping
Successive cycles of prototyping and testing, each informed by feedback from the previous iteration.
Rapid prototyping
Use of digital fabrication such as 3D printing and laser cutting to produce prototypes quickly from CAD files.
Working prototype
Functional prototype testing how a product works mechanically or electronically, beyond mere appearance.
Block model
3D foam or balsa model representing a product's mass and silhouette.
Card modelling
Used early to test form and proportion; cheap and quick.
Maquette
Small scale model from French; common in sculpture and product design.
Rapid prototyping
Quick fabrication by 3D printing or laser cutting from CAD.
Sketch model
Quick low-fidelity model in card or foam to explore form and scale.
Working prototype
Functional model used to verify mechanism and ergonomics; near final form.
Hardwood
Timber from broadleaved deciduous trees such as oak and beech, generally denser and slower-growing than softwoods.
MDF
Medium-density fibreboard made from compressed wood fibres and resin, valued for smooth surfaces and ease of machining.
Manufactured board
Engineered timber product such as MDF, plywood or chipboard, providing dimensional stability and large sheet sizes.
Plywood
Manufactured board of thin veneers glued with grain at right angles, giving strength in both directions.
Seasoning
Controlled drying of timber to reduce moisture content, minimising warping and improving workability.
Softwood
Timber from coniferous trees such as pine and spruce, faster-growing and widely used for construction and furniture frames.
Carbon footprint
Total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by a product, person or organisation, measured in CO2 equivalents.
Cradle to cradle
Design philosophy by McDonough and Braungart (2002) where end-of-life materials become inputs for new products.
Cradle to grave
Lifecycle analysis covering all stages from raw material extraction through manufacture, use and final disposal.
Embodied energy
Total energy required to produce a material or product, including extraction, processing and transport.
Life cycle assessment
Method evaluating environmental impacts of a product across its life from raw materials to disposal, standardised in ISO 14040.
Six Rs
Sustainability framework: Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair and Recycle, guiding designers towards lower-impact products.

Jigs and fixtures
Workshop aids that hold work and guide tools so repeated operations, such as drilling, are identical across a batch without marking out each part.
Quality assurance vs quality control
Quality assurance is the whole system that prevents defects; quality control is the inspection and testing of outputs against the specification.
Scales of production
One-off, batch, mass and continuous production; the expected volume drives decisions on tooling, jigs, workforce and unit cost.
Standardised components
Bought-in parts such as screws, hinges and fittings made to standard sizes, reducing cost and guaranteeing reliable, interchangeable quality.
Tolerance
The allowable variation in a dimension, stated as upper and lower limits; parts within tolerance will fit and function as intended.
